The Great Supper
SUP-er
noun phrase
From the Greek deipnon, “supper” or “feast,” the great banquet of the Lord’s parable of the gospel call.

Biblical Definition

The parable of the great supper sets forth the free and gracious call of the gospel, and the guilt of those who slight it. A certain man made a great supper, and bade many; and sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready (Luk 14:17). But they all with one consent began to make excuse: one had bought a piece of ground, another five yoke of oxen, another had married a wife, and could not come. The master of the house, being angry, sent his servant out into the streets and lanes of the city to bring in the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind; and yet there was room, so he commanded, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled (Luk 14:23). The dictionary marks this parable as a picture of God’s gracious invitation in the gospel, first to the Jews who had been bidden, and then, when they refused, to the poor and the outcast and the Gentiles in the highways. The excuses are not great crimes but lawful things loved more than Christ, and they damn as surely; for the Lord declares, None of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper (Luk 14:24). The compelling is no force upon the will, but the effectual drawing of grace, by which the unwilling are made willing and brought in.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Lord’s parable of the great feast whose bidden guests made excuse, and the poor were compelled to come in.

expand to see more

THE GREAT SUPPER, the Lord’s parable of the gospel call to a great feast.

The bidden guests all made excuse and would not come.

The master sent for the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind.

He bade his servant compel them to come in, that his house might be filled.

None of the bidden who refused should taste of his supper.

Key Scripture

Luk 14:17 — "And sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready."

Luk 14:18 — "And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused."

Luk 14:23 — "And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled."

Luk 14:24 — "For I say unto you, That none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper."

Modern Corruption

A parable of Scripture; it sets forth the free gospel call, the guilt of slighting it, and the effectual grace that compels the outcast to come in.

expand to see more

The great supper has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s great picture of the gospel feast and the call to come. The dictionary records the parable that the reader may mark both the guilt of the excusers and the grace that fills the house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel call is free and full, all things now ready, yet slighted by men who love lawful things more than Christ. The bidden made excuse and were shut out; the poor and the outcast were gathered in; and the servant was charged to compel them to come in. This compelling is no violence upon the will but the powerful, effectual drawing of sovereign grace, by which the unwilling are made willing and brought to the feast. So the parable warns that to make excuse is to perish, and teaches that all who come, come because they are drawn.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “supper,” the parable names the great feast of the gospel from which the excusers were shut out.

The Great Supper — from the Greek deipnon, “supper” or “feast.”

A man made a great supper and bade many.

The bidden guests all made excuse and would not come.

The poor and outcast were gathered in their stead.

The servant was bidden to compel them to come in.

Usage

"Like the bidden of the great supper, those who make excuse shall not taste the feast."

"Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in."

"The compelling of grace makes the unwilling willing and brings them in to the feast."
